title: Overlapping Intervals
subtitle: Complete Pattern Guide for Placement OAs
author: Mayank
overview:
Before any pattern, master this one fact: every interval problem reduces to the universal overlap check.

**Two intervals [a, b) and [c, d) overlap if and only if:** `a < d AND c < b`

They do **NOT** overlap when `b <= c` (first ends before second starts) OR `d <= a` (second ends before first starts). Negate that and you get the overlap condition above.

**For closed intervals** [a,b] and [c,d]: overlap when `a <= d AND c <= b`.
coreConcept:
**Union (merge)** = [min(a,c), max(b,d)] — use when combining overlapping intervals into one.
**Intersection** = [max(a,c), min(b,d)] — use when finding the common window for one arrow/shot.

triggerWords: "Merge all overlapping intervals", "return list of non-overlapping intervals", "insert a new interval and merge" → Pattern 1 (Sort + Merge)
"Minimum number of X to cover/burst all intervals", "remove minimum intervals so none overlap" → Pattern 2 (Greedy, sort by end)
"Maximum number of overlapping / concurrent / simultaneous X", "minimum resources (rooms, cars, workers)" → Pattern 3 (Line Sweep)
"Can one person attend all?", "return false if new booking conflicts" → Pattern 4 (Simple overlap check)
Dynamic queries: intervals added/removed at runtime, "after each operation return the current state" → Pattern 5 (Interval + Data Structure)
structureSignals: You are given an array of [start, end] pairs
Range up to 10^9 — cannot iterate over every point (line sweep)
One X covers multiple intervals only if they share a common point (intersection, not union)
Need O(log n) per operation — TreeMap or Segment Tree

variations.name: Pattern 1 — Sort + Merge Intervals
variations.coreIdea: If you sort by start time, overlapping intervals become **adjacent**. You only ever need to compare the current interval with the last merged one — a single left-to-right pass suffices.

items: You are given an array of [start, end] pairs

solved.title: Merge Intervals
solved.statement: Given an array of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals and return the result.

boxes.body: If you sort by start time, overlapping intervals become **adjacent**. You only ever need to compare the current interval with the last merged one — a single left-to-right pass suffices.

boxes.title: Interview Answer
boxes.body: "I sort by start time so that all potentially overlapping intervals are contiguous. Then a single greedy pass merges them: if the current interval's start is within the previous end, extend the end; otherwise, finalize the previous group and start a new one. This avoids the O(n^2) pair-checking of brute force."

boxes.title: Edge Cases
items: All intervals identical: return one copy
All intervals non-overlapping: return sorted input
Touching intervals [1,2],[2,3]: depends on open/closed — for closed intervals (<=) they merge to [1,3]
Interval completely inside another: [1,10],[2,5] → [1,10]; `Math.max` handles this

bruteForce.approach: For every pair of intervals, check if they overlap. If yes, merge them and restart. Repeat until no merges happen. Restarting every time is wasteful; no structure is exploited.

optimal.approach: Sort by start, then one greedy merge pass.

variations.name: Pattern 2 — Greedy Interval Scheduling (Sort by End)
variations.coreIdea: An arrow/resource can cover multiple intervals only if there is a point inside **all** of them simultaneously — that is their **intersection**. Sort by end time: the interval with the earliest end is the most constrained.

items: "Minimum number of X to cover/burst all intervals"
One X covers multiple intervals only if they share a common point (intersection, not union)
Think: "how many groups can share one resource?"

problems.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons

solved.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
solved.statement: Balloons on a number line as [x_start, x_end]. An arrow shot at x bursts all balloons covering x. Find minimum arrows to burst all balloons.

boxes.body: An arrow can burst multiple balloons only if there is a point x inside **all** of them simultaneously — that is their **intersection**. Sort by end time: the balloon with the earliest end is the hardest to include later. Always shoot at its end — this maximizes overlap coverage greedily.

boxes.title: Interview Answer
boxes.body: "I sort by end time because the balloon that closes earliest is the most constrained — if I don't shoot it now, I need a dedicated arrow. By shooting at its end, I maximize the chance of also hitting later balloons. The window I maintain is the intersection, not the union, because all balloons must be hit by the *same* arrow position simultaneously."

boxes.title: Dry Run — [[10,16],[2,8],[1,6],[7,12]]
items: **Output: 2** (Arrow 1 at x=6 bursts [1,6],[2,8]; Arrow 2 at x=12 bursts [7,12],[10,16])

boxes.title: Edge Cases
items: No overlaps at all: n arrows (one each)
One balloon contains all others: 1 arrow
Use `Integer.compare` instead of `a[1]-b[1]` in the comparator — prevents integer overflow when values approach ±10^9

bruteForce.approach: Try all possible arrow positions from 0 to 10^9. For each position, greedily burst as many balloons as possible.

optimal.approach: Sort by end; maintain the intersection window.

solved.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
solved.statement: Given intervals, find the minimum number to remove so the rest are non-overlapping.

boxes.body: Flip the thinking: **maximise the number you KEEP**. Keep as many non-overlapping intervals as possible by always keeping the one that ends earliest (leaves most room for future intervals). Answer = total - kept.

optimal.approach: Sort by end; count how many can be kept.

variations.name: Pattern 3 — Line Sweep + Difference Array
variations.coreIdea: The overlap count only **changes** at start and end points of events — not anywhere in between. So instead of checking 10^9 points, record startTime → +1 and endTime → -1, then sweep left to right. The running sum at any point = active events there; the peak running sum is the answer.

items: "Maximum number of overlapping / concurrent / simultaneous X"
"Minimum resources (rooms, cars, workers) to handle all at once"
Range up to 10^9 — cannot iterate over every point
Events have a start and an end; you need the busiest moment

solved.title: My Calendar III
solved.statement: Implement a calendar where each `book(start, end)` returns the maximum k-booking (peak number of simultaneously overlapping events) across the whole timeline.

boxes.title: Interview Answer
boxes.body: "I use a difference array because the overlap count only changes at event boundaries, not between them. With endpoints up to 10^9, I cannot iterate over every point. By recording +1 at start and -1 at end in a TreeMap (for sorted order), I reduce the problem to sweeping at most 2n critical points. The peak running sum is the answer."

boxes.title: Edge Cases
items: Identical intervals: map accumulates (e.g., `10:+2`) — handled correctly
Back-to-back intervals [1,5) and [5,10): `5:-1` and `5:+1` cancel → 0 overlap at 5 (correct for half-open intervals)
Large coordinates (10^9): TreeMap handles — no array-size issues

optimal.approach: TreeMap difference map swept on every booking.

solved.title: Meeting Rooms II
solved.statement: Given meeting time intervals, find the minimum number of conference rooms required. Same pattern as My Calendar III, classic framing: minimum rooms = peak overlap.

optimal.approach: Sort starts and ends separately, then two-pointer sweep.

variations.name: Pattern 4 — Simple Overlap Check (No Merge)
variations.coreIdea: Binary question: does any pair of intervals conflict? No aggregation needed — just detect any pairwise overlap, either by sorting once or by TreeMap floor/ceiling lookups on insert.

items: Binary question: can a single entity attend/handle all events?
No aggregation needed — just detect any pairwise overlap

boxes.title: Edge Cases
items: Booking at exact same time as an existing booking: conflict
Back-to-back [1,5) then [5,10): no conflict (half-open interval, use strict inequality)

optimal.approach: TreeMap floor/ceiling neighbours to check both sides in O(log n).
